get.summary: Cognito pool coordinates for a subdomain, for external OAuth clients.
get.description:
Cognito pool coordinates for a subdomain, for external OAuth clients.

    The MCP server (eg-pz-mcp) fronts Cognito with an OAuth 2.1 facade so
    Claude connectors can sign in. To send a user to the right Hosted UI it
    needs the pool and app client for their tenant, and pools here are
    per-company — the subdomain is the only thing that identifies one.

    This is also the entitlement gate for the connector. It is the one call
    the MCP server makes before *every* sign-in and before every token
    refresh, so refusing here both blocks new sessions and expires live ones
    within an access token's lifetime — without the MCP server needing its
    own LaunchDarkly client.

    Public by design, and safe: user pool ids and *public* app client ids are
    not credentials (any SPA authenticating against Cognito ships them to the
    browser). Deliberately excluded: the client secret, and any hint about
    whether a company exists beyond what ``/company/config`` already reveals.

post.summary: Re-invite a user who has not activated yet (admin action).
post.description:
Re-invite a user who has not activated yet (admin action).

    ZP-3916 rewrote this endpoint. It used to generate a password, make it
    permanent with ``admin_set_user_password(Permanent=True)``, email it, and —
    when SendGrid failed — return the cleartext password in its own response
    body. It now goes through Cognito's own re-invite
    (``MessageAction='RESEND'``), which mints a fresh *temporary* password and
    leaves the user in FORCE_CHANGE_PASSWORD, plus a new single-use activation
    link. No credential is generated here, returned here, or logged here.

    An already-activated user is refused rather than quietly reset: they need a
    password reset, and resetting a working account to a temporary password
    because someone clicked the wrong button is a worse outcome than an error
    message.

get.summary: Open an invitation link. Returns the masked address and the link state.
get.description:
Open an invitation link. Returns the masked address and the link state.

    Public by necessity — the recipient has no session yet. Safe because the
    token *is* the credential: without a valid one this returns nothing about
    any account, and the address it does return is masked, so a leaked link
    does not disclose the full mailbox.

    ``status`` is deliberately coarse (valid / expired / used / invalid) and
    every failure returns the same body, so the response cannot be used to
    probe which addresses exist.

post.summary: Self-service "my link expired, send me another".
post.description:
Self-service "my link expired, send me another".

    ZP-3897 requires this: an expired link must not be a dead end that becomes
    a support ticket. Public, and therefore written so it tells the caller
    nothing:

      * the response is byte-identical whether or not the address exists,
      * it is held to the same timing floor either way,
      * and it only ever acts on a user still awaiting activation, so it
        cannot be used to bounce a fresh temporary password at somebody with a
        working account.

put.summary: Require, or stop requiring, MFA for everyone in the caller's company.
put.description:
Require, or stop requiring, MFA for everyone in the caller's company.

    Scoped to the caller's OWN company, taken from their user row rather than
    from the request body. An admin of company A must not be able to set policy
    for company B by changing an id, and on a shared Cognito pool the two are
    otherwise indistinguishable at the identity layer.

put.summary: Turn Cognito's email one-time code factor on or off for the caller.
put.description:
Turn Cognito's email one-time code factor on or off for the caller.

    There is no associate/verify pair as there is for TOTP: the address is
    already on the account and Cognito owns both sending and checking the code,
    so setting the preference IS the enrollment.

    Unlike the authenticator factor, switching this OFF is allowed for the
    owner. Removing TOTP is `security.manage` because it can be someone's only
    factor; email can only be turned off here while it is not the thing
    satisfying a requirement, which the guard below enforces.

put.summary: Allow, or stop allowing, email codes to satisfy this company's mandate.
put.description:
Allow, or stop allowing, email codes to satisfy this company's mandate.

    Sibling of set_organization_mfa_policy and scoped the same way — the
    caller's own company, from their user row, never from the body.

    Turning it OFF does not un-enrol anyone. Their email factor keeps working
    as a second factor; it simply stops counting toward the requirement, so
    someone relying on it is prompted to add an authenticator. Revoking a
    factor people already depend on would lock them out mid-session.

put.summary: Require MFA for one user, over and above the organization setting.
put.description:
Require MFA for one user, over and above the organization setting.

    An escalation only. Because the flags OR together, setting this false does
    not exempt anyone from an organization mandate — that is deliberate, so an
    individual cannot be quietly carved out of a security control. Lifting a
    mandate is a change to the organization policy.

post.summary: Start enrollment for a signed-in user. Returns the secret and QR URI.
post.description:
Start enrollment for a signed-in user. Returns the secret and QR URI.

    The secret is returned to the user who is enrolling, over their own
    authenticated request, and is not persisted or logged anywhere on our
    side — Cognito holds it. It is not enabled yet; that happens in /verify.

post.summary: Confirm the first code and switch TOTP on.
post.description:
Confirm the first code and switch TOTP on.

    Both steps, one request — see cognito_mfa.complete_enrollment for why they
    are welded together.

get.summary: Is TOTP on for this user, is it required, and may they turn it off?
get.description:
Is TOTP on for this user, is it required, and may they turn it off?

    Read from Cognito rather than mirrored locally for `enrolled`: a second copy
    of MFA state is a second thing that can disagree with the one that actually
    gates sign-in. The cached column exists for the admin user list, where one
    AdminGetUser per row is not viable.

    ``available`` reports whether this tenant's pool has software-token MFA
    activated at all. A pool with it switched off cannot enrol anyone, so the
    client skips the prompt entirely rather than showing an error nobody in the
    building can fix.

    ``required`` / ``required_source`` / ``locked`` come from
    app/services/mfa_policy: the pool's own setting, then the organization flag,
    then the per-user flag, ORed. ``locked`` means the requirement is the pool's
    and no application setting can relax it.

    This response is what *applies* the requirement: the client blocks the app
    behind the enrollment prompt when ``required`` is true and ``enrolled`` is
    false. There is deliberately no server-side gate refusing other routes —
    turning an organization mandate on would otherwise break every session that
    was already open. A pool set to MfaConfiguration=ON is the case where
    Cognito itself enforces, before any token is issued.

    ``can_remove`` used to be the `security.manage` permission, and that is no
    longer what it means. ZP-3896 made removing your OWN factor self-service:
    the endpoint takes no user id and acts on the caller's access token, so
    there is no other person's factor to reach, and the mandate check refuses
    an administrator exactly as it refuses anyone else. See
    ``mfa_policy.can_remove_own_factor`` for the full reversal.

    ``remove_available`` and ``remove_unavailable_reason`` are the answer
    itself, not its inputs. Reporting only the inputs left the client to
    rebuild ``action_availability``'s table from four booleans, which is the
    hand-maintained mirror this module exists to avoid — one owner for the
    rule, or the menu and the route drift and the drift is invisible.

post.summary: Turn off your own authenticator app.
post.description:
Turn off your own authenticator app.

    Self-service, restored under ZP-3896 after ZP-3915 deleted it. Worth
    knowing why it is back, because the reasons for removing it were good ones
    and only one of them has changed.

    It was deleted because it "appeared to turn 2FA off and did not": under an
    organization mandate it cleared the factor and the user was prompted to
    enrol again at the next sign-in. That is fixed here rather than argued
    with — ``ACTION_REMOVE_OWN`` refuses under a provider or organization
    mandate, so the control is only ever offered where removal actually sticks.
    It was also faulted for writing two kinds of state at once; this writes one,
    the factor, and never touches ``users.mfa_required``.

    What changed is that there is now a reason a user needs this. A passkey and
    a conventional MFA factor are alternatives in Cognito, not companions: any
    configured MFA factor withdraws every passwordless sign-in option, passkeys
    included. Without a way to turn the authenticator off, a user who enrolled
    in TOTP can never use a passkey — see docs/ZP-3896_PASSKEY_AND_MFA.md.

    **This is self-targeted by construction.** It takes no user id and acts on
    the caller's own access token, so no permission gate is needed to stop it
    reaching somebody else's factor — there is no target to name. Removing
    another person's authenticator remains POST /users/<id>/mfa/reset, which is
    ``security.manage``, a different action with different rules (reset is
    recovery and is deliberately allowed under a mandate).

    The code in the body is step-up proof, not enrollment. Possession of the
    factor being removed is evidence that the holder of this session owns the
    account; without it, a stolen session strips the victim's second factor
    silently and permanently. (An earlier version of this paragraph said
    Cognito has no "recently authenticated" primitive. It does — ``auth_time``
    is a default access-token claim. It is not used here because whether a
    refresh re-stamps it is unverified; see passkey_remove_v4.)

    Only the authenticator is touched. A user with the email factor as well
    keeps it, still ``Enabled`` and therefore still challenged — the same
    decision cognito_mfa.admin_reset documents, and for the same reason: naming
    ``EmailMfaSettings`` at all is refused outright by a pool below the
    Essentials feature plan, so re-preferring the survivor would break removal
    on every pool that has no email MFA. The consequence is worth stating
    plainly to the user, because it is counter-intuitive: removing TOTP does
    NOT re-enable passwordless for someone who also has email MFA on.

get.summary: Which sign-in methods this organization offers.
get.description: Sign-in methods this ORGANIZATION offers, in the order the sign-in screen should list them. Public, and deliberately takes no email: an answer that varied per user would report whether an account exists and which factors it holds. A method appears only when the organization allows it AND its Cognito pool can perform it, so the list is safe to render directly. `password` is always present unless an administrator has explicitly retired it.

post.summary: Begin a passkey sign-in. Returns the WEB_AUTHN challenge, or a refusal.
post.description: Begin a passkey sign-in. Returns a `WEB_AUTHN` challenge whose `challenge_parameters.CREDENTIAL_REQUEST_OPTIONS` is passed to `navigator.credentials.get()`. Send the assertion to /auth/v4/respond-to-challenge as `credential` with `challenge_name: "WEB_AUTHN"`; on success that call returns tokens and NO further challenge — a passkey is both factors, so a second-factor screen on this path is a bug. A device with no passkey is refused exactly like a wrong one: fall back to /auth/v4/email-code/start rather than reporting why.

400.description: `method_unavailable` — passkeys are not enabled for this organization, or its pool cannot perform them. Returned even when no UI offered the method: the server is authoritative, not the screen.

401.description: `passwordless_start_failed` — the sign-in cannot start. Covers an unknown address, an account with no registered passkey, and a pool that declined the factor, ALL with the same body and the same elapsed time. Do not attempt to distinguish them; offer another method.

post.summary: Begin an emailed-code sign-in — the fallback when a passkey is not usable.
post.description: Begin an emailed-code sign-in — the fallback when a passkey is not usable. Cognito sends and verifies the code; answer the returned `EMAIL_OTP` challenge at /auth/v4/respond-to-challenge with `code`. Same factor the account may already use as a second step, now allowed to start an authentication. Non-enumerating on the same terms as /auth/v4/passkey/start: an unregistered address is answered identically and no mail is sent.

post.summary: Options for creating a passkey on this device.
post.description: Options for creating a passkey on the current device, from Cognito's `StartWebAuthnRegistration`. Authenticated: registering a passkey acts on a session, it does not create one. Pass `credential_creation_options` to `navigator.credentials.create()` and send the result to /auth/v4/passkey/register/complete. Cognito owns the credential; nothing about it is stored by this API.

400.description: `method_unavailable` — the pool has no WebAuthn configuration, so no passkey can be registered against it.

post.summary: Register the credential the device just created.
post.description: Register the credential the device just created. Send the object from `navigator.credentials.create()` as `credential`; a JSON string is accepted too. Never logged by this API.

get.summary: Passkeys registered on this account, for the security page.
get.description: Passkeys registered on the calling account, for a security page. Reported from Cognito rather than mirrored locally. Credential ids are deliberately not returned — they identify an authenticator. An account with no passkeys and a pool that cannot list them both return an empty list: in each case the right next step is to offer to register one.

post.summary: Delete one of this user's own passkeys.
post.description:
Delete one of this user's own passkeys.

    Self-targeted by construction, and not by choice: Cognito's
    ``DeleteWebAuthnCredential`` takes an ``AccessToken`` and has no ``Admin``
    variant, so a credential can only ever be removed by the person who owns
    it. An administrator cannot do it for them, which is worth knowing before
    anyone is told support can clean this up.

    **Deliberately no policy gate.** Unlike turning off an authenticator, this
    is not refused under an organization or provider mandate. Revocation has to
    stay possible whatever the policy says — the passkey you most need to remove
    is the one on the device you just lost, and a mandate is not a reason to
    keep a credential alive on a stolen laptop. The same reasoning covers
    ``passkey_allowed``: an organization that switches passkeys off later must
    not strand its users with credentials they cannot revoke.

    Nor is deleting the last one refused. It is not a lockout: PASSWORD stays in
    every pool's ``AllowedFirstAuthFactors``, so the user signs in with their
    password, and under a mandate they meet the enrollment prompt and set up a
    factor again. Refusing would protect nobody and would block the one case
    this exists for.

    **No step-up proof, and that is a gap rather than a decision.** The
    sibling route above, ``remove_totp_v4``, demands possession of the factor
    it is about to remove, on the reasoning that a stolen session must not be
    able to strip a victim's second factor silently and permanently. That
    reasoning applies here with more force than it does there, not less: the
    sweep configures every pool with ``MULTI_FACTOR_WITH_USER_VERIFICATION``,
    which makes the passkey the user's second factor, so deleting it IS an MFA
    removal for anyone whose passkey is their only factor.

    It is not gated here because gating it alone would close the smaller hole
    and leave the larger one open. ``passkey_register_start_v4`` and
    ``passkey_register_complete_v4`` take a bare session too, so a stolen
    session's first move is to enrol the ATTACKER's own device — durable
    access that survives the stolen session and satisfies MFA on its own.
    Against that, revoking a victim's credential is the lesser capability.
    The same is true of ``verify_totp_v4``: across this file, factor removal
    for TOTP is the only account-security mutation that asks for anything
    beyond a valid access token.

    Closing it properly means one rule over the whole factor lifecycle —
    enrol, replace, revoke — not a check bolted onto the one route a review
    happened to look at. Cognito does expose the primitive: ``auth_time`` is a
    default access-token claim ("the authentication time, in Unix time format,
    that your user completed authentication") and is already decoded into
    ``request.cognito_user``, so a freshness window costs no round trip and no
    password prompt. What is NOT yet established is whether Cognito re-stamps
    ``auth_time`` when tokens are refreshed. If it does, a freshness check buys
    nothing, because holding a session is holding a refresh token. That must be
    measured before anything is built on it — it is the whole load-bearing
    assumption. Tracked separately; do not treat this docstring as a claim that
    the current state is safe.

    Cognito owns the credential, so there is nothing of ours to clean up —
    ``users.mfa_enrolled`` tracks the authenticator app, not this.

get.summary: Where to send the user to sign in with Google.
get.description:
Where to send the user to sign in with Google, plus the `state` to hand back on return. Navigate the browser to `authorize_url`.

Pass `consent=true` only AFTER the user has agreed, on a confirmation screen, to connect their Google account to their existing Egalvanic account. The flag travels inside the signed state, so it cannot be claimed by a client that never asked. Without it a first-time link is refused a session — see /auth/v4/google/exchange.

The PKCE verifier is deliberately not returned: the server holds it against this state and spends it during the exchange.

ZP-4640: `authorize_url` is a Google URL when this deployment has the direct flow configured, and the pool's Hosted-UI URL otherwise. Either way the user returns to the tenant's `/auth/callback` and the client calls /auth/v4/google/exchange — clients must not inspect or depend on the URL's host.

200.description: The URL to navigate to and the state to echo back.

400.description: `method_unavailable` — Google is not enabled for this organization, or its pool cannot run the configured flow (no Google identity provider on the Hosted-UI flow; no custom-auth triggers or `ALLOW_CUSTOM_AUTH` on the direct flow).

get.summary: Google's redirect target for the direct flow (ZP-4640).
get.description:
ZP-4640. Google's redirect target for the direct flow — the ONE redirect URI registered on the brand's Google OAuth client, served on our own domain so Google's account chooser names it instead of a pool's amazoncognito.com host. Not called by clients.

Checks the signed `state` and 302-redirects the browser to the tenant's `/auth/callback` carried inside it, with `code` and `state` (or `error` and `state` when the user cancelled) unchanged. That page then calls /auth/v4/google/exchange as usual. Spends nothing and signs nobody in. The forward target must be https on a host in `GOOGLE_CALLBACK_ALLOWED_HOSTS`.

400.description: `google_failed` — the state is missing, forged, from the Hosted-UI flow, or names a host outside the allowlist.

post.summary: Finish a Google sign-in, or explain what is still needed.
post.description:
Finish a Google sign-in, using the `code` and `state` from the redirect. Three outcomes:

* **200 with tokens** — signed in. The identity was already linked, or it was a first link the user consented to before the handoff.
* **200 with `requires_link_confirmation: true`** — the address matches an account this Google identity has never been linked to, and no consent travelled with the return. NO session is issued and NO link is created. Show the confirmation dialog naming `masked_email`, then start the flow again with `consent=true`.
* **401 `google_failed`** — no matching account, an address Google has not verified, or a stale or forged state. One message for all of them, and no account is created in any case: a Google identity may link to an existing account and may never bring one into being.

200.description: Signed in, or awaiting link confirmation.

400.description: `method_unavailable` — Google is not enabled for this organization.

401.description: `google_failed` — the sign-in cannot be completed. Do not attempt to distinguish the reasons; offer another method.

post.summary: Clear a user's authenticator app (ZP-3916).
post.description:
Clear a user's authenticator app (ZP-3916).

    The recovery path for a lost or wiped device. Cognito software-token MFA has
    no backup codes, so until ZP-3897's second story lands this is the only way
    back into an account whose authenticator is gone.

    Two properties keep it from being an authentication bypass:

      * it issues nothing — no session, no token, no password. The user's next
        sign-in is password-only, and their next visit to security settings
        starts a fresh enrollment;
      * it is permissioned (``security.manage``), scoped to the caller's own
        company by ``@require_same_company_user``, and audited with both the
        actor and the target.

    ``security.manage`` rather than the broader ``users.manage``: touching
    somebody else's second factor is an administrative security act, not user
    administration, and the same bar applies whether the target is a company
    user or an account (portal) user — both are ``users`` rows in the caller's
    company. Only Super Admin and Admin hold it.

    What this does NOT do: delete the registered software token. Cognito has no
    API for that — ``AdminSetUserMFAPreference`` clears the *preference* and the
    verified secret stays registered, so the old authenticator is still the most
    recently associated one. Anyone holding both the lost device and the password
    could sign in (password-only after a reset, by design) and re-enable MFA from
    that same secret.

    Nothing here limits that any more. A global sign-out used to, by revoking
    the sessions the lost device already held; it went under ZP-4120, because
    changing or resetting a second factor is not meant to end anybody's session
    — the target's or the caller's. The comment on the call site records the
    decision and the trade in full. Displacing the secret itself
    requires a fresh ``AssociateSoftwareToken``, which only the user can do. So
    until ZP-3897's backup-code story lands, "reset" means "force
    re-enrollment" and nothing more: existing sessions survive it, the
    registered secret survives it, and the account is password-only until the
    user enrols again.

post.description:
Server-side paginated + filtered user list for a company.

    Body:
      {
        "page": 1,
        "page_size": 25,
        "search": "",              # global free-text across name/email/jobtitle/role
        "filters": {               # per-column free-text (all optional)
          "name": "",              # first/last/username
          "email": "",
          "jobtitle": "",          # the users.role column (job title)
          "roles": "",             # RBAC role name (joined via user_roles/roles)
          "status": ""             # 'active' | 'inactive' (free text)
        },
        "sort_by": "created_at",   # name|email|jobtitle|status|created_at|modified_at
        "sort_dir": "desc"         # asc|desc
      }

    Response: {success, data: {items, total, page, page_size}}.

    Filtering / searching / sorting / counting / pagination all run in SQL.
    Per-user enrichment (roles, labor types, SLD access) is computed only for
    the page_size rows returned — matching the GET endpoint's row shape.

    The existing GET /users/company/<id> endpoint is intentionally left
    unchanged; this is an additive v2.

post.summary: Platform Users: the company's internal (T1) users on approved domains
post.description:
Same body, filters, sorting, paging (default 25, max 100) and row shape as `POST /users/company/{company_id}/v2`, scoped to users with no live guest-portal seat whose email domain is approved for the company (company domain + exceptions + egalvanic.com / bces-iq.com). Guest-portal users are listed by `GET /users/guest-portal`.

`filters.domains` (list or comma-separated) narrows to selected approved domains; an unapproved value is ignored, and a request naming only unapproved domains returns no rows.

Extra response field: `available_domains` (the approved list, the filter's options). With `"with_counts": true` in the body it also returns the filter-chip counts, taken under the status filter only: `domain_counts` ({domain: n}), `domains_total`, and `excluded_total` — T1 users left out because their email domain is not approved (they appear on neither Platform Users nor Guest Portal Users). Overlapping domains (`acme.com` + `ops.acme.com`) count a user under each, so `domain_counts` can sum past `domains_total`.

200.description: A page of platform users plus the domain filter data.

post.summary: Users v3 - v2 plus a structured, server-side RBAC role filter.
post.description:
Users v3 - v2 plus a structured, server-side RBAC role filter.

    Body is v2's, with one difference: ``filters.roles`` selects roles instead
    of free-texting over the role name. It accepts a role name or role id, a
    list of either, or a comma-separated string, and OR-combines them: a user
    matches if they hold ANY of the selected roles. A single value is just the
    one-element case, so single- and multi-select from the frontend take the
    same path.

      {
        "page": 1,
        "page_size": 25,
        "search": "",
        "filters": {
          "name": "", "email": "", "jobtitle": "",
          "roles": ["Administrator", "Technician"],   # or "Administrator",
                                                      # or a role UUID / list of UUIDs
          "status": ""
        },
        "sort_by": "created_at",
        "sort_dir": "desc"
      }

    page_size}} with the same per-row keys - so the grid needs no
    response-side change. ``/users/company/<id>/v2`` is left untouched.

post.summary: Create an IR photo row — legacy (keys chosen by the client) or create-first (keys minted here)
post.description:
Three request shapes, told apart by the body.

**1. Legacy — WITH `ir_photo_key` / `visual_photo_key`** (the FLIR camera app, the iOS uploader, the typed asset form): the client chose the keys and uploads under `{ir_session_id}/{key}` (`POST /s3/url {bucket: 'ir_photos', key, operation: 'write'}`). Unchanged: an upsert on `id`; FLIR-IND rows get `{key}_visual`; answers `{success, ir_photo}` (201). The row is stamped with the asset's IR / IR Checklist service in the work order (`service_id`) when one is registered there.

**2. Work-order upload — `{ir_session_id, original_filename, ir_sha256}`, NO `node_id`, NO keys** (the web's "Upload IR Photos"; `X-Direct-Write: true`; one call per picked file). The asset is unknown to the client, so the file is matched by its stem — case- and extension-insensitive — against the names typed in the asset form on that work order's live rows: the IR side (`ir_photo_key`) or the visual side (`visual_photo_key`). An IR-side match gives the row its flat `storage_key` (minted now when absent), `original_filename` and `content_sha256` — the file is the IR; a visual-side match gives it `visual_storage_key`. `ir_sha256` dedupes first: the same bytes already registered on a row of this work order → that row, `created: false`, `ir_upload` only if the bytes never landed. A file no row names is a 400 `{error: 'no row in this work order names this file', errors[]}`; a name whose row already holds DIFFERENT uploaded bytes is a 409. After the PUTs call `POST /ir_photo/extract_visual/batch {photo_ids}` for the entries with `extract_visual: true`.

**3. Create-first with `node_id`** — `{node_id, sld_id, id?, ir_session_id?, original_filename?, ir_sha256?, visual_file_name?, type?, date_created?, service_id?}`: a NEW row, keys minted. `ir_session_id` null (or the asset's pseudo id) = outside a work order (`direct_entry: true`); a real one must be reachable with the asset in it (404) and stamps the asset's IR / IR Checklist service there (a client-named `service_id` must be one of those — 400). Re-posting the same `id` is idempotent: same keys, URLs for whatever is still missing.

**Response for 2 and 3** (201): `{success, ir_photo: {…row incl. id, node_id, storage_key, visual_storage_key, display_key, visual_display_key, original_filename, service_id, direct_entry}, created, ir_upload: {bucket, key, url, expires_in} | null, visual_upload: {…} | null, extract_visual, data: {id, storage_key, visual_storage_key, ir_upload, visual_upload, created, extract_visual, ir_session_id, service_id, direct_entry}}`. `created` = this call registered the file (a row inserted, or a key minted on a typed row); false when the bytes were already registered. Errors: 400 `{error, errors[]}`, 404 (asset / work order not reachable), 409, 502 (S3 refused to presign).

**Storage (task #133).** Every IR photo's files live in ONE flat repository keyed by the photo's own id — `ir-photos/{company_id}/{ir_photo_id}/ir.{ext}` (the camera's radiometric file, never overwritten), `visual.{ext}` (extracted, or the client's own visual), `edited.jpg` (the web editor's output) — stored whole on the row as `storage_key` / `visual_storage_key` / `edited_storage_key`. `ir_photo_key` / `visual_photo_key` are display names; `original_filename` is the camera's file name. Rows written by the FLIR camera app, the iOS uploader and the typed asset form keep the legacy layout `{ir_session_id}/{ir_photo_key}` (all three storage columns null) until a file is attached to them. **Clients read `display_key` (the edit when there is one, else the IR file) and `visual_display_key`**, and presign them with `POST /s3/urls/batch`: a flat key is exact (`find_by_prefix: false`, or true — an extension-bearing key passes through verbatim either way); a legacy key is an extension-less stem (`find_by_prefix: true`).

400.description: Bad body, or (work-order upload) no row in this work order names this file

404.description: Asset / work order not found or not reachable

201.description: Legacy: `{success, ir_photo}`. Create-first / work-order upload: the entry above

409.description: `id` exists on another row, or a different file is already registered as this photo

Answers `{success, ir_photo, extraction?}`.

**Create-first body** (no keys — task #133): the same as `POST /ir_photo/create`'s create-first shapes, plus `type`. Extraction needs the bytes, which the client PUTs AFTER this answer, so it runs only when the IR object is already there (a re-post of the same `id` after the PUT): otherwise the 201 carries `extraction: {pending: true, reason}` and the client re-posts, or calls `POST /ir_photo/{id}/extract_visual` / `/extract_visual/batch`.

post.summary: Register IR photos on an asset outside a work order (and presign their uploads)
post.description:
The direct-entry twin of the work-order upload. ONE call creates the `ir_photos` rows and answers with presigned PUT URLs; the client then PUTs the files and finishes with `POST /ir_photo/extract_visual/batch` (`photo_ids` = the ids whose `extract_visual` is true).

**Body** `{photos: [{ir_file_name, ir_sha256, visual_file_name?, id?, date_created?, type?}]}` — 1..500 entries. `ir_file_name` / `visual_file_name`: the camera's file names (basename, ≤255 chars, `.jpg` / `.jpeg` / `.png`). `ir_sha256`: the IR file's SHA-256, 64 hex. `id`: a client-minted row id for offline replay. `date_created`: ISO-8601 (default now). `type`: `IR` (default) or `VISUAL` (a visual-only capture — the one file is the visual, no radiometric key is minted).

**Storage (task #133).** Every IR photo's files live in ONE flat repository keyed by the photo's own id — `ir-photos/{company_id}/{ir_photo_id}/ir.{ext}` (the camera's radiometric file, never overwritten), `visual.{ext}` (extracted, or the client's own visual), `edited.jpg` (the web editor's output) — stored whole on the row as `storage_key` / `visual_storage_key` / `edited_storage_key`. `ir_photo_key` / `visual_photo_key` are display names; `original_filename` is the camera's file name. Rows written by the FLIR camera app, the iOS uploader and the typed asset form keep the legacy layout `{ir_session_id}/{ir_photo_key}` (all three storage columns null) until a file is attached to them. **Clients read `display_key` (the edit when there is one, else the IR file) and `visual_display_key`**, and presign them with `POST /s3/urls/batch`: a flat key is exact (`find_by_prefix: false`, or true — an extension-bearing key passes through verbatim either way); a legacy key is an extension-less stem (`find_by_prefix: true`).

**What the server does.** Mints the row's flat keys (`ir_session_id` null, `direct_entry: true`), keeps the camera's stem as `ir_photo_key` and its name in `original_filename`. Without `visual_file_name` the row is FLIR-IND-like: `visual_photo_key` is `{stem}_visual`, `visual_storage_key` is `visual.jpg` and the extraction routes fill it from the radiometric file after the upload (`extract_visual: true`). With one it is FLIR-SEP-like: the visual gets its own presigned URL and nothing is extracted.

**Dedupe.** An `ir_sha256` that already exists on a live photo of this asset outside any work order returns THAT row (`created: false`) instead of a second one; if its bytes never landed (`ir_upload_status` finds no object) fresh URLs come back so the client can finish — `ir_upload` / `visual_upload` are null when nothing is to be uploaded. Two entries with the same hash in one call collapse to one row. A replayed `id` of THIS asset's flat photo is the same create (same keys, URLs for whatever is still missing); any other existing `id` is 409.

**Tenancy.** The node must be the caller's company's and a site the caller can reach — 404 otherwise; the body names no tenant (the folder's company is the caller's). Requires `ir_photos.upload`. Work-order screens never show these rows; the asset page (`GET /node/{id}`) and the site sync bundle (`GET /sld/v3/{sld_id}` → `ir_photos[]`, selected by site) carry them with `direct_entry: true`. Rows task #132 filed under the asset's pseudo work-order id keep it and still read as direct.

The site's work orders, as the Reports screen needs them (ZP-4422).

    A separate route rather than paging /sld/<id>/sessions, for two reasons.
    That endpoint returns every work order at the site in one response, and
    its callers rely on that unpaged shape. And it returns the whole Session row: 26 fields,
    of which this screen reads seven. Work blocks, asset scope, photo prefixes
    and plan links were being serialised for every work order at the site and
    thrown away in the browser.

    Paging, search and the closed-only filter are all applied HERE, in one
    query, because they cannot be split. Filtering after paging makes page
    sizes lie — ask for ten rows, render six — and searching after paging
    reports "no match" for records sitting on a page the client never fetched.

    ?limit=   1..100, default 25
    ?offset=  >= 0, default 0
    ?q=       matches the work order name OR its service type name
    ?closed_only=true  only work orders with a close date

    Ordering is newest first on the date the screen shows, so the row a user
    is looking for is on page one.

get.summary: ZP-3117: edges only. The NFPA70E tables/dashboard and WorkUnitsTab
get.description:
ZP-3117: edges only. The NFPA70E tables/dashboard and WorkUnitsTab
    used to call GET /sld/<id> (the full-dependency loader — photos, IR,
    sessions, issues, quotes, tasks, comments, mappings) and discard
    everything but the edges array. On large SLDs that full load was
    observed taking 59-1000s in QA and starving the task into ALB
    health-check kills. This returns just the edges (one query — terminal
    relationships are lazy='joined').

get.summary: Get SLD with all dependencies (v3). Same as v2 but includes edges
get.description:
Full site graph (v2 plus edges with a null source or target).

**ZP-4010:** the payload now also carries `routes[]` — every recorded route of the site, plus tombstones from the last 90 days (a soft-deleted route arrives with `is_deleted: true` and an empty `stops[]`), so a device that ingests the site graph also learns about routes deleted elsewhere and can abandon its runs on them. Older tombstones are deliberately NOT here: this is the full-dependency payload, and deleted routes would accumulate in it forever — a device offline longer than the window catches up through `GET /api/route/site/{sld_id}?include_deleted=true`, which is unbounded.

The key is present only for callers holding **`routes.view`** — this endpoint is gated on `slds.view`, so the key would otherwise hand route data to roles that were deliberately not granted `routes.*`. It is OMITTED, not emptied, so "not allowed" is never reported as "no routes". Each entry is the same `RouteDto` that `GET /api/route/site/{sld_id}` returns.

**Task #107:** each `ir_sessions[]` entry carries `service_check_dates` beside `service_checks` — `{node_id: {service_id: "YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ"}}`, WHEN that service was checked off for that asset in that work order (the latest `session_method_lines.executed_at` stamp across the service's live lines, UTC). Mobile derives an asset's maintenance history from it offline, grouping by its own local day. A pair that was never stamped is absent — including one `service_checks` reports true through the legacy node-grain check-off — and a work order with no stamps sends `{}`. Also on `GET /api/sld/v2/{sld_id}`.

post.description:
Task #97: the current state of just the named nodes / edges of ONE site
    — what a realtime client re-fetches after a change signal.

    Body: {"node_ids": [...], "edge_ids": [...],      (each ≤ 500)
           "shape": "v2" | "canvas",                  (default "v2")
           "view_id": <uuid|null>, "include": ["links"]}

    shape "v2" (the iOS app's SwiftData upsert): /sld/v2 dicts, deleted rows
    included so deletes apply.
    shape "canvas" (the GoJS editor): EXACTLY what a fresh canvas load returns
    for these ids — /sld/{id}/graph dicts in All Nodes, /sld-view/{v}/graph
    dicts (view positions, collapse, manips, simplified redirects, reference
    nodes) for a view — plus the edges touching the named nodes, and
    gone_node_ids / gone_edge_ids for the ones no longer on that canvas
    (deleted, or not in the view). Built from the same code as the full load,
    so an applied delta can't drift from a reload.

    Scoped to the site: company AND site access via caller_can_reach_sld.

get.summary: ZP-2210: derive a node's voltage context.
get.description:
ZP-2210: derive a node's voltage context.

    Returns two views of the same node:

    - ``inherited`` — the SLD-graph-derived voltage (lazy resolution
      from the nearest source-class or transformer-class ancestor).
      Used for the asset form's read-only voltage display on
      non-boundary nodes.
    - ``effective`` — the breaker's effective circuit voltage (L-L vs
      L-N vs HLD wild leg) combining the inherited panel voltage with
      pole count, phase wire configuration, and (for HLD) circuit
      position. Used by the SKM frame matcher.

    Both share the same upstream walk; this endpoint surfaces the full
    derivation block so the FE can render "Inherited from <source>"
    breadcrumbs.

post.summary: Presign several S3 objects at once (exact keys, or extension-less stems by prefix)
post.description:
`{operation: read|write, find_by_prefix?: bool, items: [{bucket, key}]}` → `{results: [{bucket, key, original_key, url, public_url} | {…, error}], total, operation}`.

`find_by_prefix: false` (default) presigns every key EXACTLY as sent — the path for a flat IR photo key (`display_key` / `visual_display_key` / `storage_key` / `edited_storage_key`, task #133). `find_by_prefix: true` resolves a READ key WITHOUT an extension by prefix to the object really there (`IR1` → `IR1.JPG`; never a sibling) — the path for a legacy `{ir_session_id}/{ir_photo_key}` stem; an extension-bearing key passes through verbatim there too, so one call can mix both.

post.summary: Add a fluid sample to an asset (optionally in a work order)
post.description:
**Work orders (task #109).** `session_id` in the body makes this the `DGA` service's evidence for the asset in that work order: the caller must be able to open the work order and the asset must be in it (404 otherwise). The record is stamped with `session_id` and `service_id` — the asset's `DGA` service there, or the `service_id` the body names, which must be one of them (400); `service_id` stays null when the asset carries no `DGA` service in that work order. Without `session_id` it is an asset-page record and belongs to no work order.

**Issues.** A work-order record raises its own Fluid Sample Anomaly issue — once — the first time its `overall_band` is `caution` or `poor` (IEEE C57.104 Condition 2+ for the gases, the C57.106 limits for the physical / chemical and furan values); priority Critical at Condition 4, High when poor, else Medium. Checked on create and on every update, because lab values usually land on the work order's sample after the visit. A sample that later grades clean keeps its issue for a person to close. The new issue's id comes back as `issue_id` and the issue carries `origin.source = "fluid_sample"`. Asset-page records never raise one on their own; `POST /api/fluid-samples/{row_id}/issue` raises it on request.

**Offline replay.** `id` may be a client-minted uuid. A create whose `id` already exists answers 409 `record id already exists` — the replaying device then sends the same body as a `PUT`.

get.description: The reading types a client may offer, in render order — each with its `key`, `label`, `unit`, `points` (in order), `min` / `max` of one value and `has_rating` (true for `current`: `rating_amps` applies and `percent_load` is derived). Also `rating_amps` bounds, `load_points` (the points percent load is taken over), `max_decimals`, `notes_max_length` and `sources`. The catalog lives in code; render from it rather than hard-coding a type.

get.summary: An asset's readings, newest first
get.description:
The asset's live readings ordered by `taken_at` descending (the 200 most recent), every type together, in and out of work orders (`session_id` says which). `default_rating_amps`, beside `data`, is the asset's own current rating — what a new current reading's rating starts at; null when the asset records none.

**A reading.** `reading_type` is one of the catalog's types (`GET /api/readings/vocabulary`: `current` in A at points A, B, C, N; `millivolt_drop` in mV at A, B, C, N; `voltage` in V at A-B, B-C, C-A — companies cannot define types). `unit` is the type's unit. `values` holds one `{point, value}` per MEASURED point, in catalog order. `taken_at` is ISO-8601 UTC. `technician` is the name snapshot of `technician_user_id`, set by the server. `source` is `manual` or `issue_backfill` (lifted from a Thermal Anomaly issue's old tables; `source_issue_id` names the issue; editable like any other).

**`percent_load`** is computed by the server, for `current` readings only: the highest of phases A / B / C (never N) ÷ `rating_amps` × 100, to one decimal; null when there is no rating or no phase value. Clients render it and never recompute it.

The same readings ride the site sync bundle (`GET /api/sld/v3/{sld_id}` → `readings[]`), where soft-deleted ones are included with `is_deleted: true`. A node outside the caller's company reads as 404.

post.summary: Add a reading to an asset (optionally in a work order)
post.description:
Body: `{id?, session_id?, service_id?, reading_type, taken_at?, technician_user_id?, rating_amps?, notes?, values: [{point, value}]}`. `taken_at` defaults to now. For a `current` reading an OMITTED `rating_amps` is filled from the asset (`default_rating_amps`); an explicit null records the reading without a rating.

**Rules (400 with `error` + `errors[]`, never a 500).** `values` is an array of `{point, value}`: every point must belong to the type (matched ignoring case) and may appear once; a `value` of null or `""` means not measured and is not stored; at least one point must carry a number; numbers (JSON numbers or plain numeric strings) must lie within the type's `min`..`max` from the vocabulary (0..100,000 A, 0..1,000,000 mV, 0..1,000,000 V) and are kept to 3 decimals. `taken_at` is an ISO-8601 date-time (a bare date is refused; no zone = UTC), not before 1950 and not after tomorrow. `rating_amps` (current readings only; ignored on the other types) is greater than 0 and at most 100,000. `notes` is at most 2,000 characters. `technician_user_id` must be a user of the caller's company; null clears the technician.

**Work orders.** `session_id` says the reading was taken in that work order: the caller must be able to open it and the asset must be in it (404 `Work order not found` / `Asset is not in this work order`). The reading is stamped with the asset's `IR` service there, else its `IR Checklist` service, else `service_id` stays null — a reading does NOT need a service. A `service_id` the body names must be one of those (400). Without `session_id` it belongs to no work order — and so does a `session_id` equal to the asset's direct-entry pseudo id (the `ir_session_id` / `session_id` a `direct_entry: true` IR photo or ultrasonic scan carries): stored with `session_id` null, no reachability or membership check.

**Offline replay.** `id` may be a client-minted uuid. A create whose `id` already exists answers 409 `record id already exists` — the replaying device then sends the same body as a `PUT`.

Requires `nodes.manage`.

get.summary: An asset's thermal baseline: key components with their observations, and the per-photo analysis state
get.description:
`data.components[]` — the asset's live key components in `sort_order`, each with `observations[]` newest first; `data.analyses[]` — one per analysed IR photo (`status` queued / running / done / failed, `model`, what the model said about the equipment, `summary`, `error`, `started_at` / `finished_at`). `?include_deleted=1` also lists hidden components (`is_deleted: true`) so a client can offer to unhide them.

**Boxes** are `[x1, y1, x2, y2]` in PERCENT of the THERMAL frame (0..100, origin top-left, x1 < x2, y1 < y2). The thermal frame is the radiometric map (640×480 on an E96); the visual the model saw is cropped to exactly that frame, so the same box addresses both the IR and the aligned visual.

**A component** is one of the asset's key parts (lug, fuse clip, breaker column …) with an identity that outlives one photo: `reference_ir_photo_id` / `reference_box` say where it was first found; `origin` is `ai` or `user`; `sort_order` is the model's listing order. `temp_rule` says which stored statistic is the component's charted temperature, by `surface`: `median` for `insulated` / `painted` (robust to a hotter background in the box's corners), `center` for `bare_metal` (the 5×5 sample at the box centre — the part itself, with the low-emissivity caveat), `max` for `other`.

**An observation** is that component on one IR photo: `box`, and the temperatures CODE read inside it from the raw radiometric data — `temp_center` (mean of the 5×5 pixels at the centre), `temp_median`, `temp_max`, `temp_mean`, all °C to one decimal — plus `temp`, the one under the component's `temp_rule` (chart this one). `method` is `ai` (found on this photo), `ai_refind` (re-found against the reference) or `user`; `confidence` 0..1 is the model's own; `taken_at` is the file's capture time (UTC), else the photo's `date_created`; `session_id` is the photo's work order when it has a real one (null for a direct-entry photo). Observations are listed newest first. The model never produces a temperature, and temperature is never a reason to list a component.

Three queries, no per-row reads. A node outside the caller's company reads as 404. Guest-reachable (read only).

post.summary: Run the AI over the asset's IR photos (synchronous)
post.description:
Body `{ir_photo_ids?: [uuid, …]}` — at most 10; omitted → every live IR photo of the asset WITHOUT a `done` analysis, oldest first, capped at 10. Explicit ids may name already-analysed photos (a re-run replaces that photo's observations; components stay). Ids that are not this asset's live photos → 400.

Runs SYNCHRONOUSLY, one photo at a time: ~12 s per photo (one model call; the first photo of an asset creates its components, every later one is sent with the reference photo(s) and their numbered boxes and re-finds them), so ten photos take about two minutes — show progress and keep the request open. The photos' analysis rows are claimed `running` under a per-asset lock first; a second call for the same asset while one runs is 409 `thermal_analysis_running` (with `running_ir_photo_ids`) until it finishes or its claim ages past 5 minutes (a crashed run is then marked `failed` and re-claimed).

Response `data`: `analyzed[]` (photo ids that finished), `failed[]` (`{id, error}` — one photo failing never fails the call), `created_component_ids[]`, `timings[]` (`{ir_photo_id, seconds, model_seconds, usage}`), plus the same `components[]` / `analyses[]` as the GET. Nothing to analyse → 200 with empty lists and a `message`. Requires `nodes.manage`; records `node.thermal_analyzed`.

**Boxes** are `[x1, y1, x2, y2]` in PERCENT of the THERMAL frame (0..100, origin top-left, x1 < x2, y1 < y2). The thermal frame is the radiometric map (640×480 on an E96); the visual the model saw is cropped to exactly that frame, so the same box addresses both the IR and the aligned visual.

**A component** is one of the asset's key parts (lug, fuse clip, breaker column …) with an identity that outlives one photo: `reference_ir_photo_id` / `reference_box` say where it was first found; `origin` is `ai` or `user`; `sort_order` is the model's listing order. `temp_rule` says which stored statistic is the component's charted temperature, by `surface`: `median` for `insulated` / `painted` (robust to a hotter background in the box's corners), `center` for `bare_metal` (the 5×5 sample at the box centre — the part itself, with the low-emissivity caveat), `max` for `other`.

**An observation** is that component on one IR photo: `box`, and the temperatures CODE read inside it from the raw radiometric data — `temp_center` (mean of the 5×5 pixels at the centre), `temp_median`, `temp_max`, `temp_mean`, all °C to one decimal — plus `temp`, the one under the component's `temp_rule` (chart this one). `method` is `ai` (found on this photo), `ai_refind` (re-found against the reference) or `user`; `confidence` 0..1 is the model's own; `taken_at` is the file's capture time (UTC), else the photo's `date_created`; `session_id` is the photo's work order when it has a real one (null for a direct-entry photo). Observations are listed newest first. The model never produces a temperature, and temperature is never a reason to list a component.

post.summary: Add an ultrasonic scan to an asset (outside a work order, or in one)
post.description:
Same body as `POST /ir_session/{sid}/ultrasonic-scans` minus `node_id` (the asset is in the URL), plus an optional `session_id`.

**Outside a work order** — `session_id` absent, or equal to the asset's direct-entry pseudo id (the `session_id` a `direct_entry: true` scan carries): the scan is filed under that pseudo id, with no membership check and `service_id` null (a `service_id` in the body is a 400 — there is no work order for it to be on). A non-normal `result` still mints the Ultrasonic Anomaly issue on the asset, as a plain asset issue (no work order). Files for such a scan are uploaded through `POST /node/{node_id}/ultrasonic-scans/upload` BEFORE the create, with the client-minted `id` as `scan_id`; their keys (`image_key` / `audio_key`) must sit under `ultrasonic/{pseudo id}/{scan id}/`.

**In a work order** — a real `session_id`: the work-order path (the caller must reach it, the asset must be in it, the asset's UT service is stamped).

Edits and soft-deletes go through `PUT /ultrasonic-scans/{id}` either way: for a direct scan the gate is the asset's site, not a work order. The asset's history (`GET /node/{node_id}/ultrasonic-scans`) and the site sync bundle (`ultrasonic_scans[]`, selected by node) carry direct scans with `direct_entry: true`. Requires `ir_photos.upload`; a node outside the caller's company / site is 404.

Whether the asset page shows Fluid Samples (`fsa`), Torque Records (`torque`) and Ultrasonic (`ut`). A section shows when the asset already has records of that kind, or when a service that feeds that kind evaluates to the asset — the same rule walk that scopes a work order (the procedure on the asset's class, rules in order, first match wins, an empty method list is out of scope). Fluid samples and torque records are fed by a matched method whose form carries that record block, or by any matched method of a `DGA` / `TV`-type service (task #109); ultrasonic by any matched method of a `UT`-type service. Services are the company's own plus the globals it has not forked.

This replaces the retired `fsa_eligible` / `torque_eligible` flags on node classes and subtypes. Those are no longer accepted on write and nothing on the server reads them; they are still returned, frozen, only so app builds from before this change keep their sections — do not build on them. post.description:
Establish a PM program on one or more assets of the SAME class.

    Body, one of two shapes:
      {node_ids, pm_plan_id, service_dates?, service_due_dates?,
          last_completed?}
        — copy the plan's service cadences onto every asset.
      {node_ids, node_class_id, lines: [{service_id, interval, recurring?,
          implementation_method_ids?, last_completed?, next_due?}],
          service_dates?, service_due_dates?, last_completed?}
        — compose the program directly. implementation_method_ids pins the
          methods; omitted/empty means the materializer resolves them at
          work-order time.

    Last-serviced dates: user-supplied dates (service_dates {service_id:
    YYYY-MM-DD}, per-line last_completed, or the blanket last_completed) are
    recorded as STATED HISTORY (asset_service_history — they survive program
    changes), then each (asset, service) resolves its effective last-serviced
    as the later of stated history and the service-method registry's
    check-off stamps. due_date is (effective or today) + interval months —
    so in bulk, each asset's own history sets its own due dates.

    Next-due dates: the OTHER way to anchor a service. service_due_dates
    {service_id: YYYY-MM-DD} (or per-line next_due) schedules the first
    occurrence directly — it lands in user_due_date, the same column the
    bulk cadence editor writes, with the same semantics: taken at face
    value (never shutdown-snapped), standing until the service is performed
    on/after it, after which the cadence resumes from the completion. A
    line may carry both — a stated date is a FACT about the past, a next
    due is a DECISION about the future.

    Two write modes (body.mode):
      replace (default) — the assets' existing live schedules are soft-deleted
        and the new program written in their place: "make these assets' program
        THIS" (a PM plan, a copied program).
      merge — the program editor's mode. The list of lines IS the edit: a line
        already on an asset is UPDATED in place (interval / recurring / pinned
        methods / next due, whichever were sent; provenance kept), a line the
        asset lacks is INSERTED — unless the line's `scope` is 'existing', in
        which case assets without it are left alone (an untouched or merely
        re-tuned line on a mixed selection must not spread to assets that never
        had it). `remove_service_ids` soft-deletes those services (by family)
        across the selection. Nothing else on the assets is touched.

post.summary: Take assets off their PM program: soft-delete their live schedules.
post.description:
Take assets off their PM program: soft-delete their live schedules.
    Body: {node_ids}.

put.summary: State (or clear) the customer's last-known service date for one
put.description:
State (or clear) the customer's last-known service date for one
    service on one asset. Body: {service_id, last_serviced_on} — a null
    last_serviced_on clears the stated entry. Registry evidence is untouched
    either way; the effective value stays the LATER of the two, so stating a
    date earlier than a recorded work order changes nothing downstream.
    Returns the asset's recomputed history.

put.summary: Whether this asset may be de-energized for maintenance. Body:
put.description:
Whether this asset may be de-energized for maintenance. Body:
    {shutdown_restriction, shutdown_cadence_years} — the cadence (years
    between expected shutdown windows) is required for
    planned_shutdowns_only and cleared otherwise. Gates de-energized
    services at program-apply time; existing schedules are not rewritten.

get.summary: The site's maintenance program as a time grid: every scheduled service
get.description:
The site's maintenance program as a time grid: every scheduled service
    occurrence — completed, due now, scheduled or planned — bucketed by
    month/quarter/year.

    ?sld_id=      (required) the site
    ?preset=      year | 3y | 5y | history | all   (each sets a default axis)
    ?axis=        months | quarters | years   (overrides the preset's axis)
    ?from= &to=   explicit window (YYYY-MM-DD)
    ?group_by=    asset (default) | class | location | service
    ?service_id= &location= &com= &asset_class= &parent= &planning_status=
                  filters; each may REPEAT for a multi-select
                  (location values: room:<uuid> | text:<free text>)
    ?limit= &offset=                  asset-mode paging
    ?q=<text>                         free-text asset search (label or class)
    ?include_filters=1                also return the filter option lists
    ?include_derived=1                …including the graph-derived menus
                                      (power scheme, voltage — a 1.5 s walk)
    ?include_totals=1                 also return the four stat-card counts
    ?include_unprogrammed=1           every asset on the site (the editor) — also
                                      returns `planning` (site-wide status counts)

get.summary: What comes due on this site inside the horizon, grouped by service.
get.description:
What comes due on this site inside the horizon, grouped by service.

    ?sld_id= (required) &days= (default 90, max 400).

    Grouped by SERVICE across the whole window rather than by month: a work
    order is a visit, and "Infrared Thermography, 24 assets, 15 Sep – 20 Nov"
    is a decision a planner can make. Every asset carries its own due date and
    room, so the client can regroup by room without another round trip.

post.summary: Turn a selection of upcoming work into work orders.
post.description:
Turn a selection of upcoming work into work orders.

    Body: {sld_id, orders: [{name, due_date?, lines: [{service_id,
    node_ids: [...]}]}]}. One work order per entry; several lines in one entry
    IS a multi-service work order, which needs no special support — a work
    order's type is derived from the services on its method lines.

    Each line carries its OWN assets rather than the order sharing one list:
    a service must only reach the assets it is actually due on. Sharing the
    union would evaluate thermography against the UPS units that rode along
    for their own service and quietly add work the program never asked for.

    Each order is created and then scoped through add_assets_to_work_order,
    the same evaluation the create-WO wizard's scope step runs, so method
    lines, forms and completion all behave exactly as a hand-built work order
    does. Assets a service's rules don't match still join, and come back in
    `unmatched`.

post.summary: Set the shutdown rule on MANY assets at once.
post.description:
Set the shutdown rule on MANY assets at once.

    Same validation as the per-node PUT — planned_shutdowns_only requires a
    cadence, and clearing to unrestricted/never drops it — but as ONE statement,
    because shutdown policy is a property of a room or a process, not of an
    individual panel: it is almost always decided for a whole group.
    Body: {node_ids, shutdown_restriction, shutdown_cadence_years?}.

post.summary: State (or clear) a last-serviced date for ONE service across MANY assets.
post.description:
State (or clear) a last-serviced date for ONE service across MANY assets.

    The date is the same for every asset in the call — this is for "we did the
    whole switchgear room in March", which is how stated history actually
    arrives. Per-asset dates stay the asset tab's job.

    A null last_serviced_on clears the stated entry. Registry evidence is
    untouched either way: effective last-serviced is the LATER of the two, so
    stating a date earlier than a recorded work order changes nothing
    downstream. Body: {node_ids, service_id, last_serviced_on}.

post.summary: What stated history already exists across a set of assets, per service.
post.description:
What stated history already exists across a set of assets, per service.

    The bulk history editor needs to SHOW before it lets anyone add or delete:
    stating a date is an assertion about the customer's site, and overwriting
    or dropping one blind is how a record quietly becomes wrong. One row per
    service, with how many of the selected assets carry a stated date and the
    span those dates cover — a single date when they agree, a range when they
    do not. Body: {node_ids}.

post.summary: What the selected assets' LIVE programs prescribe, per service — the
post.description:
What the selected assets' LIVE programs prescribe, per service — the
    bulk cadence editor shows before it lets anyone change: one row per
    service with how many assets carry it and the interval mix ("every 6 mo
    on 42, every 12 mo on 3"), plus how many already carry a user-set next
    due. Body: {node_ids}.

post.summary: Edit ONE service's cadence across the selected assets' live programs —
post.description:
Edit ONE service's cadence across the selected assets' live programs —
    the applied plan is a starting point, not a contract.

    Body: {node_ids, service_id, interval?, next_due?}. Presence-keyed:
      - interval: new months between occurrences (bounds-checked).
      - next_due: YYYY-MM-DD sets a USER next-due — the next occurrence lands
        exactly there and the cadence steps from it; null CLEARS a previous
        user date (derived scheduling resumes). Taken at face value, never
        snapped to the shutdown grid: the user is looking at a calendar.
    At least one key required. Only live schedule rows are touched — assets in
    the selection whose program doesn't carry the service are counted in
    `skipped_no_schedule`, never invented rows (adding a service is /apply's
    job). Family-aware on service_id, like every other service membership
    test. Provenance (source_pm_plan_id) is kept: the plan is still where the
    program CAME from, even customized.

put.summary: Where the planning of this asset's program stands. Body:
put.description:
Where the planning of this asset's program stands. Body:
    {planning_status: none | need_more_information | plan_ready}. A plain
    user-set flag — it does not touch the program, and nothing sets it but
    this route and the bulk one.

post.summary: Set the planning status on MANY assets at once — "these twelve all need
post.description:
Set the planning status on MANY assets at once — "these twelve all need
    a condition assessment before anyone can plan them" is said about a
    selection, not one panel at a time. Body: {node_ids, planning_status}.

post.summary: Apply one condition-calculator result to MANY assets.
post.description:
Apply one condition-calculator result to MANY assets.

    The calculator asks about criticality, operating conditions and
    maintenance history — questions that are usually answered the same way for
    a whole room or a whole class of gear, which is why it belongs in the bulk
    editor and not only on one asset at a time.

    Body: {node_ids, com: 1|2|3|4|null, com_calculation}. `com` 4 is the
    non-serviceable verdict (the calculator's, or a direct pick) — a
    COMPLETED assessment whose com_calculation carries
    `maintenance_value: null`. NULL com = not assessed.

post.summary: Re-date the condition assessment on MANY assets without re-answering
post.description:
Re-date the condition assessment on MANY assets without re-answering
    the calculator.

    An assessment older than ASSESSMENT_VALID_DAYS reads as expired on the
    Condition Assessment page. When a crew has in fact looked the gear over
    again and found nothing changed, the honest fix is to record WHEN they
    looked — not to walk the calculator again for the same three answers
    (Eric, 2026-09-07). Only the stamp moves: `com` and `com_calculation` are
    untouched.

    Body: {node_ids, assessed_on: 'YYYY-MM-DD'}. Assets with no calculator
    assessment are skipped — there is nothing to date — and reported.

get.summary: Per-node BFS-derived attributes for a site: power scheme and voltage.
get.description:
Per-node BFS-derived attributes for a site: power scheme and voltage.

    Neither is a column — power scheme is the source that feeds the asset
    (UPS > Generator > Utility, from SLDController.compute_power_scheme) and
    voltage is walked from the voltage authorities — so any surface that wants
    to FILTER on them needs them served rather than read. The Condition
    Assessment grid holds its whole site client-side, so one call here lets it
    filter on the same things the Maintenance Program does without a
    round-trip per change.

    Both walks are O(N·E); this endpoint is the explicit opt-in, same as
    ?include_filters on the program grid. ?sld_id= required.

get.summary: Live compliance diff for a site (?pm_standard_id= to compare against a
get.description:
Live compliance diff for a site (?pm_standard_id= to compare against a
    specific standard; defaults to the company's NFPA 70B 2026 ladder).
    Pipeline-key callable — the compliance report's dataprep reads this, the
    same SSOT-over-HTTP contract the AF report uses.

get.summary: Hypothetical resolution: for every asset on the site and each
get.description:
Hypothetical resolution: for every asset on the site and each
    ``?service_ids=a,b,c``, the implementation methods the service's rules
    would select (first match wins, computed system voltage, SKM device
    facts, company fork precedence). The EMP Lite report's Appendix D reads
    this via the pipeline key so the lambda never reimplements the matcher —
    see app/services/emp_method_resolution.py.

get.summary: The STANDARD's prescription per asset (Eaton-5 visualizer): what the
get.description:
The STANDARD's prescription per asset (Eaton-5 visualizer): what the
    chosen PM standard says each asset should get, and how often — never
    what happened. One row per asset the standard prescribes for (buses and
    non-serviceable assets excluded, same as the compliance engine), each
    with its expected services and intervals; plus the service legend and the
    location / class facets the tab filters on.

    ?pm_standard_id= as on GET /program-compliance/<sld_id> (defaults to the
    company's ladder). Read-only, computed on the fly from `_expected_pairs`
    — nothing is stored.

Acknowledge deviations: {dev_keys: [..], justification, expires_on?}.

get.summary: Everyone in the company, flagged with whether they can see this account.
get.description:
Everyone in the company, flagged with whether they can see this account.

    has_access here means the ACCOUNT is visible to them (owner or internal
    mapping) — site access within it is the site-level list's business.

    Top-level can_share mirrors the WRITE authority: revoking here strips
    minted site rows, so it is owner/admin only (see revoke_account_access),
    and the client uses the flag to render the toggles read-only for
    everyone else rather than letting them 403.

post.summary: Map a user into the account (visibility grant, type_id stays NULL).
post.description:
Map a user into the account (visibility grant, type_id stays NULL).

    Owner/admin only, like the revoke (review round 4): the plain gate admits
    anyone auto-mapped off a single site grant, which made membership
    self-propagating — each grantee could grant further, and an Account
    Manager grantee gains session scope over every site of the account.
    Everyone else extends visibility the intended way: share a site they
    hold the share right on, and the cascade mints the mapping.

delete.summary: Unmap a user from the account AND retire their system-minted site
delete.description:
Unmap a user from the account AND retire their system-minted site
    rows — a site-access write, so it demands owner/admin authority
    (review round 3: behind the visibility gate, any auto-mapped user or
    portal seat could strip a colleague's real access). The owner cannot
    be revoked here — ownership is a different concept; reassign the owner
    instead.

get.summary: Everyone in the company, flagged with whether they can open this site.
get.description:
Everyone in the company, flagged with whether they can open this site.

    Top-level can_share reports whether the CALLER may grant/revoke here, so
    the client can disable the toggles instead of round-tripping to the
    write endpoints' 403.

post.summary: Assign a user to the site; the account mapping cascades automatically.
post.description:
Assign a user to the site; the account mapping cascades automatically.

    Writes require the SHARE right (can_user_reassign_sld: admin, the account
    owner, or an explicit grant with can_reassign), not mere access — the
    service path enforces the same contract, and gating on access alone let
    any technician with one non-reassignable site hand it to the whole
    company. Reading the list still only needs access.

delete.summary: Deactivate a user's explicit assignment to the site.
delete.description:
Deactivate a user's explicit assignment to the site.

    Same share-right gate as granting (see grant_sld_access), EXCEPT
    self-removal: leaving a site you were assigned to needs no share right —
    that worked before the gate and stays supported. Access that flows from
    ownership can't be revoked here — there is no row to deactivate and the
    rule would re-derive it anyway.

get.summary: Accounts with their sites nested underneath — the Customers tree.
get.description:
Accounts with their sites nested underneath — the Customers tree.

    THREE grouped queries, not a count per row: accounts, then sites, then one
    grouped COUNT over nodes. A company with a few hundred sites would otherwise
    issue a query per site to label it.

    Sites you can't access are NOT shown (no greyed-out rows — Eric,
    2026-08-25). The site set is ``get_accessible_slds_for_user`` (explicit
    assignments + sites of owned/portal accounts; admins see everything), so
    this endpoint introduces NO new access boundary — it re-presents one that
    already exists. An owned account therefore shows all of its sites, a
    merely-mapped account only the ones you were assigned. Accounts are scoped
    to the company of the AUTHENTICATED user, never to anything in the request.

    Accounts with no accessible site are still returned, with an empty list and
    a zero count: for an owner that genuinely means "this customer has no sites
    yet", and hiding the row would make the customer look deleted. Sites whose
    account_id is NULL come back under the ``unassigned`` bucket rather than
    being dropped — the Sites tab showed them, so omitting them here would
    silently lose rows.

    ZP-4151: a site linked to several accounts is returned under EVERY account
    it belongs to, and each site carries ``account_ids`` (primary first). One
    site can therefore appear in more than one bucket, so the bucket totals sum
    to more than the number of distinct sites — counting rows across buckets
    double-counts. This is intended, and the frontend handles a site appearing
    under multiple account nodes.

    ``/customers/tree/v2`` is a SEPARATE, paginated handler further down and
    carries the same ``account_ids`` shape. This route stays unpaginated for
    existing clients; new callers should use v2.

get.summary: Paginated, server-side-searched Customers tree.
get.description:
Paginated, server-side-searched Customers tree.

    Query params:
      ``limit``   1..100, default 25 — accounts per page
      ``offset``  >= 0, default 0
      ``q``       free-text, matched against BOTH account name and site name

    Response::

        {success, accounts: [...], total, limit, offset, has_more, q}

    ``total`` is the number of ACCOUNT rows matching the query (including the
    synthetic "Unassigned sites" bucket when it matches), so the client can
    render an accurate "1-25 of N" without holding the whole tree.

    THE PAGE UNIT IS AN ACCOUNT, NOT A ROW. An account comes back with its
    sites complete, because a customer split across two pages is not a thing
    the tree can draw — the user would expand a row and see only some of its
    sites, with no indication the rest were on the next page.

    Search semantics deliberately mirror what the client filter did, because
    this replaces it and a silent change in matching behaviour is worse than
    no change at all:
      * account name matches  -> account kept with ALL of its sites (the
        question was about the customer)
      * site name matches     -> account kept with ONLY the matching sites,
        and ``auto_expand`` set so the client can open it without re-deriving
        the reason it was kept
    A match on either side is enough; ``q`` is matched case-insensitively as a
    substring (ILIKE %q%), the same rule as the JS ``includes()`` it replaces.

    ZP-4151: a site linked to several accounts is returned under EVERY
    account it belongs to, and each site row carries ``account_ids`` (primary
    first). ``site_count`` is therefore per-bucket, and summing it across
    accounts double-counts shared sites. ``total`` still counts ACCOUNT rows,
    so paging is unaffected.

    ACCESS IS UNCHANGED. The visible site set is still
    ``get_accessible_slds_for_user`` and accounts are still company-scoped to
    the AUTHENTICATED user under the same owner/mapped rule as v1. This
    endpoint introduces no new access boundary and must not start — paging is
    a presentation concern, so it is applied strictly AFTER scoping.

get.description:

    badge counts per nav entry):

      - zero_value_draft: a live draft quote (legacy or v2 plan) still at $0.

        falling back to the opportunity's modified_at).

        accounts (admins: whole company).
      - site_no_assets: an accessible SLD with zero nodes.
      Users:
      - user_no_labor_types: AGGREGATE — how many active users have no labor
        types mapped (they can't be assigned to work orders). One item, not one
        per user.
      Planned work (accepted v2 plans, unreleased workorders):
      - planned_work_overdue: the scheduled window already started.
      - planned_work_upcoming: the window starts within 30 days.
    Response: {success, count, items: [{type, ...type-specific fields}]}.

post.summary: ZP-1839 — Phase 1a of the v2 SKM import.
post.description:
ZP-1839 — Phase 1a of the v2 SKM import.

    Parse + classify + resolve eqp_lib for every component in a posted
    XML payload. Returns a summary (counts, by-class, by-type,
    per-component classification + eqp_lib summary, warnings) so the
    FE can render a pre-commit review screen. **No DB writes.**

    Accepts either:
      1. Multipart form: ``xml_file`` (required) + ``sld_id`` (required)
      2. JSON body: ``{"xml_s3_key": "...", "sld_id": "<uuid>"}``

    On the multipart path the XML gets uploaded to S3 under
    ``skm-import/preview/<uuid>.xml`` and the returned ``token`` is
    that S3 key. The FE round-trips the token to /commit to actually
    write nodes + edges.

    Returns ``{token, summary}`` where ``summary`` is the dict from
    :func:`app.services.skm_xml_commit_service.preview_skm_xml`.

post.summary: ZP-1839 — Phase 1b of the v2 SKM import.
post.description:
ZP-1839 — Phase 1b of the v2 SKM import.

    Takes a ``token`` previously returned by ``/skm/import-xml/preview``
    (which is the S3 key of the staged XML), re-parses + re-classifies
    + re-resolves (deterministic — same result as preview), then writes
    Node + Edge rows in a single transaction. Mirrors ``eqp_lib`` into
    each node's first-class columns (ampere_rating / sensor_amps /
    plug_amps / frame_amps / pole_count / trip_type_id / etc.) via
    :func:`derive_first_class_fields` so the imported assets are
    fully populated for downstream consumers (arc-flash, TCC,
    coordination).

    Body JSON:
        {
          "token": "skm-import/preview/<uuid>.xml",
          "sld_id": "<uuid>",
          "default_building_id": "<uuid>"?,
          "default_floor_id":    "<uuid>"?,
          "default_room_id":     "<uuid>"?,
          "skm_namespace":       "<name>"?
        }

    ``skm_namespace`` is the SKM project name the user confirmed on the
    review screen (prefilled from the preview's ``skm_namespace.suggested``).
    Duplicate SKM ids only merge within one namespace.

    Location triple is all-or-nothing — pass all three to land the
    nodes under a specific room, or omit to leave room_id NULL (the
    legacy bulk-upload semantics).

    Returns the commit-summary dict from
    :func:`app.services.skm_xml_commit_service.commit_skm_xml`.
